dhq:abstract.p: This article presents a methodological case study of Chinook, a tool employed by the Canadian government’s department known as Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada . Chinook assists officers with temporary resident visa applications. To examine this tool, we use design fiction, a research-through-design method that builds speculative prototypes in order to explore the social, ethical, and political implications of technological systems and infrastructures. Given the system's ambiguity, fragmented documentation, and limited public accountability, we adopt speculative reconstruction as a critical and interpretive approach. This article relied on court affidavits, Access to Information and Privacy releases, and legal commentary, to develop a design fiction prototype and accompanying explainer video to visualize Chinook’s “Decision Maker” module. Through iterative sketching, prototyping, and annotation, the project translates bureaucratic and legal evidence into accessible interface logics. By anchoring speculation in the documentary record rather than in the imagination, and by directing it at an operational bureaucratic system rather than an emerging technology, the article reframes design fiction as a method of evidentiary reconstruction, revealing how digital infrastructures encode discretion and standardization within government decision-making.

dhq:teaser.p: How do you examine a government decision-making tool the public is not allowed to see? We rebuilt Chinook, the interface IRCC officers use to process visa applications, from court affidavits and access-to-information releases. Having to draw the system turned out to expose things its own documentation never acknowledges.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: How can we study tools used to manage people that are not made public? In this article we will discuss the design fiction approach we took to understand Chinook, an Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) tool used to deal with temporary resident visa (TRC) applications.

IRCC is the Canadian federal government department responsible for immigration, refugee resettlement, and citizenship, to manage high volumes of TRV applications. A TRV is the document required of foreign nationals from visa-required countries who seek to enter Canada for a temporary stay, whether as visitors, students, or workers, and IRCC processes these applications at visa offices worldwide. IRCC describes Chinook as an interface to a suite of modules that streamline decision-making using spreadsheet-based tools, and claims it does not use artificial intelligence, algorithms, advanced analytics, or built-in decision-making algorithms (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2024, 2021a, 2021b; Tao, 2022).

What is publicly known about Chinook stems from a patchwork of heavily redacted Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) requests, court affidavits, court cross-examinations, and policy commentary. These include the Ocran v. Canada litigation materials, as well as the ATIP-obtained Chinook training manuals (Daponte, 2021a, 2021b; Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a). Ocran v. Canada was a case for judicial review of a visa denial decision in which the role of Chinook was at issue. Such cases are heard by the Federal Court of Canada, which reviews decisions made by federal departments including IRCC. In response, IRCC filed an affidavit in July 2021 by Andie Daponte, an official at the department, setting out how the tool had been developed and how its modules operate. Daponte was subsequently cross-examined on that affidavit. Together these two documents remain the most detailed account of Chinook that the department has placed on the public record, and they anchor much of the reconstruction that follows.

Legal experts and advocates, such as Tao (2022), have raised concerns about several of Chinook's features: batch refusal capabilities, which allow an officer to issue refusal decisions for many applications in a single action; standardized refusal templates, which supply pre-written reasons that officers select rather than compose; and the deletion of working notes that once formed part of the procedural record. We will return to these.

This lack of available documentation presents both a methodological and ethical challenge. How does one critically examine a government decision-making tool that is shielded from public inquiry in a way that is both accurate and can engage the public? Our research responds to this challenge by turning to design fiction. Design fiction is a research-through-design method that creates speculative prototypes to explore the social, ethical, and political implications of technological systems. Developed within critical design and futures studies, it situates artifacts in plausible near-future or alternative present contexts, allowing researchers and audiences to ask “what if” questions where empirical observation is limited or impossible (Dunne and Raby, 2013; Coulton et al., 2017; Blythe, 2014; Lukens and DiSalvo, 2011). We argue that design fiction functions as a methodological bridge between limited public documentation and speculative critique, enabling critical insight into black-boxed bureaucratic systems and potentiating a new public conversation.

Our contribution to design fiction is twofold. First, design fiction has conventionally proceeded from imagination, extrapolating from trends or provocations to build artifacts that could plausibly exist. We instead anchor every speculative move in public documentation: court affidavits and cross-examination transcripts, ATIP-released training materials, and Federal Court rulings. Speculation begins only where the documentary record stops, and we mark that boundary explicitly rather than allowing evidence and invention to blur, using color-coded annotation in the prototype to distinguish elements grounded in disclosed material from those inferred from textual description. Second, design fiction has largely been directed at emerging technologies, asking what living with them might entail. We direct it instead at an existing bureaucratic system that is already operational and already producing consequences for applicants, but whose workings are withheld from the people it governs. The object of speculation here is not a possible future but a concealed present. Taken together, these two moves reposition design fiction as a method of evidentiary reconstruction, suited to institutions that are documented but not disclosed.

These two contributions have a consequence worth flagging early. Because we were building something rather than writing an argument, we kept running into decisions that a written critique could have left open. Every text field had to go somewhere and every button had to do something, so each time the documents were vague, silent, or contradictory, we had to take a position anyway. We treat these moments of friction as findings, and we report them as we go, because they show where the bureaucracy's own logic becomes visible.

It is also crucial to note that design fiction is not about predicting the future or claiming factual accuracy. Rather, it constructs plausible representations to expose assumptions, surface risks, and invite public reflection (Lindley and Coulton, 2016; Galloway and Caudwell, 2018; Barendregt and Vaage, 2021). These are our goals in this article and the associated animation we provide of Chinook based on design fiction. Our reconstruction pursues them in the manner design fiction has always pursued them, by building an artifact that can be examined and argued with rather than by making an argument alone. Where design fiction more often asks what an emerging technology might make possible, we ask instead what an existing institution has already made routine. The literature we turn to next establishes the conceptual grounds for this work: plausibility rather than accuracy as the measure of a speculative artifact, world-building as a means of synthesizing heterogeneous evidence, and reflexivity about interpretive limits. Our case extends that literature by testing whether those commitments hold when the artifact is reconstructed from a documentary record rather than imagined.

This article proceeds in five parts. First, we outline the conceptual foundations of design fiction. Second, we describe our method of reconstructing Chinook through speculative prototyping. Third, we analyze the evidentiary and narrative logic behind each module’s reconstruction. Fourth, we reflect on the epistemological implications of this method. Finally, we consider the broader potential of design fiction for studying algorithmic governance, the use of computational systems to administer and shape public decision-making (Galey, Ruecker, and Ruecker, 2010; Hinrichs et al., 2018), and deepening collective understanding.

div.head: The Conceptual Foundations of Design Fiction: Considering the Literature
div.p: Design fiction has emerged as a critical method within human-computer interaction, speculative design, and digital humanities, enabling researchers to interrogate sociotechnical systems through imagined futures and material speculation. Building on the foundational work of Dunne and Raby (2013), design fiction is specifically defined by its capacity to challenge normative assumptions and stimulate civic imagination through plausible but unreal artifacts and systems. Their notion of “social dreaming” recasts design as a critical and speculative act (also see Farias et al., 2022), rather than a utilitarian one, shifting attention from solutions to consequences.

This framework has since expanded to include a broader array of epistemological and methodological concerns. Auger (2014) argues that speculative design, when grounded in everyday material practices, allows users and designers to imagine what living with emerging technologies might actually entail. This aligns with Gaver’s (2012) provocation that research through design should not seek generalizable knowledge in the traditional scientific sense, but instead generate rich interpretive insights through engagement with concrete artifacts.

Design fiction is particularly effective for investigating opaque or black-boxed systems, such as government decision-making software, where technical schematics or source code are unavailable. Barendregt and Vaage (2021) helpfully frame speculative design as a form of “thought experiment,” positioning it within a tradition of philosophical inquiry that emphasizes inference and critique over verification. In this model, plausibility becomes the primary metric, grounded not in internal coherence alone but in the alignment between speculative reconstruction and publicly accessible fragments of documentation.

The “world-building” capacity of design fiction has also become central to its recent development (Coulton et al., 2017; also see Crabtree et al., 2025, p. 2). Coulton et al. (2017) describe this as a way to synthesize disparate evidentiary forms, such as legal testimony, user manuals, and government briefings, into coherent interface logics. The methodological stakes of this approach are significant: rather than claiming definitive knowledge about a system’s functionality, design fiction acknowledges the partial and interpretive nature of such reconstructions, while making those interpretive boundaries explicit through annotation, commentary, and visual distinction.

Still other scholarship addresses the narrative and discursive dimensions of design fiction. Blythe (2014, 2017) emphasizes the role of storytelling and character development in transforming abstract system behavior into lived experience. His work explores how fictional case studies, when well-grounded in context, can illuminate ethical concerns and systemic contradictions that would otherwise remain buried in institutional jargon. The use of characters with names familiar to many Canadians like “John” and “Alex” in the accompanying Chinook explainer video produced through design fiction (2025) reflects this tradition, offering viewers an accessible way to encounter the inner workings of a decision-making system otherwise hidden from public view. The use of fictional scenarios and characters in speculative production reflects this tradition.

Design fiction also opens up possibilities for participatory critique. Farias, Bendor, and Van Eekelen (2022) discuss how participatory speculative design encourages collective sense-making around future sociotechnical imaginaries. This collaborative orientation expands the utility of design fiction beyond individual authorship or institutional critique, embedding it within broader conversations about public agency, civic accountability, and alternative policy futures. Tsekleves et al. (2022) likewise demonstrate how speculative design has been used in Malaysia as a tool for inclusive policy development, suggesting its relevance beyond Western contexts and across diverse political regimes.

Synthesizing different bodies of literature, we found that design fiction scholarship has focused on emerging technologies and participatory imagination; however, it has rarely been used for evidentiary reconstruction of existing, hidden state systems. We should also clarify that the transformative question of “what if” is not exclusively a design fiction one; it is also a question that is being frequently asked in interdisciplinary fields such as design justice and critical infrastructure studies. Design justice, for instance, answers the question of “what if” to provide essential ethical frameworks to include marginalized communities and challenge the multiple social classifications (such as race, gender, class, and sexual orientation), which Patricia Hill Collins describes as the “matrix of domination” (see Costanza-Chock, 2020). Similarly, critical infrastructure studies expand this perspective and show how a specific infrastructure can be beneficial and functional for some while structurally hostile and broken for others (Liu, 2026). Costanza-Chock (2020) demonstrates that by using the methods of speculative design, practitioners can break free from present-day resource constraints to engage in “radical visioning.” This allows us to propose and prototype alternative technologies that do not yet exist, and build a sustainable, pluriversal world where many worlds fit (Costanza-Chock, 2020; Liu, 2026).

Finally, design fiction demands reflexivity. Galloway and Caudwell (2018) stress that such work must be evaluated not by how closely it approximates reality, but by how clearly it communicates its commitments, stakes, and interpretive limitations. By foregrounding its methodological boundaries and limitations, a speculative reconstruction like Chinook becomes an invitation to question how power, automation, and discretion are encoded into systems, especially those that shape outcomes in areas that can have negative consequences for disempowered groups such as immigration, policing, and public services.

div.head: The Practice of Design Fiction
div.p: Having defined design fiction, we now turn to how it works in practice and why it suits the study of an opaque system like Chinook. In this project, we adopt design fiction as a critical method for examining Chinook, a system that, as Tao (2022) and Daponte (2021a) point out, is intentionally shielded from public scrutiny.

Chinook’s technical infrastructure, decision-support features, and user interfaces have never been fully disclosed. Key documents remain redacted, and officers' working notes are regularly deleted, leaving minimal audit trails (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a; Daponte, 2021b). Standard forms and refusal templates reduce variation in decision-making but obscure how discretion is exercised in practice (Tao, 2022). While some public-facing commentary and policy disclosures exist, they are often fragmented, delayed, or contradictory (Colosi, 2023; Zahid, 2022). This evidentiary gap between what is observable and what is withheld calls for a method that can responsibly speculate from the margins.

Design fiction allows us to work within these margins. Rather than reverse-engineering Chinook from leaked source code or unauthorized access, we construct speculative prototypes grounded in publicly available but partial evidence: affidavits, court testimony, refusal letter samples, and Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP)-disclosed training materials (Daponte, 2021a, 2021b; Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a, 2021b; Tao, 2022). In Canada ATIP requests concerning government information subject to the Access to Information Act may be made by citizens, permanent residents, any person residing in Canada, corporations, and of course may be made by legal counsel. These sources combined form the evidentiary spine of the reconstruction, allowing us to anchor fiction in fact while marking all interpretive leaps. The result is not a simulation, but a provocation, a way to represent how the system might function in ways that demand scrutiny (Gaver, 2012; Galey, Ruecker, and Ruecker, 2010).

To provide a concrete overview of how we implemented this method, we first organized Chinook's known components into a modular map, a diagram setting out the system's constituent modules and the relationships between them, based on disclosed documentation. We then prototyped selected modules in Figma, a collaborative digital design platform suited for interface modeling and interaction mapping (Figma, 2019). Design conventions were drawn from both public sector user interfaces and commercial decision-support tools. Where documentation was missing, we generated visual structures and interface behaviors, meaning the ways in which screen elements respond to user action, such as what happens when a toggle is switched or how a refusal field is populated, that matched the logic described in testimonies or legal analyses. For example, the batch refusal templates or indicator management flags (Tao, 2022; Daponte, 2021a). These speculative components were explicitly marked and explained in our accompanying documentation. In the prototype, color-coded annotations distinguished between interface elements grounded in evidentiary screenshots (in blue) and those inferred from textual descriptions (in red), with each component cross-referenced to its evidentiary source. At no point was factual ambiguity concealed; rather, we treated it as a design constraint that demanded transparency and annotation (Blythe, 2017; Coulton et al., 2017).

div.p: Design fiction, in this context, operates as both a critique and a heuristic. It critiques the opacity of digital bureaucracy by revealing how even stripped-down systems can shape outcomes through interface defaults and workflow design (Galloway and Caudwell, 2018; Lindley and Coulton, 2016). It also offers a heuristic approach to studying inaccessible systems, an alternative to traditional audit methods when researchers lack insider access or traceable logs (Zimmerman et al., 2007; Farias et al., 2022). To operationalize this approach, we draw on the available evidence base for Chinook, mapping sources that could inform its speculative reconstruction.

div.head: Evidence Base and Source Mapping in Chinook
div.p: The design fiction prototype of Chinook was constructed using publicly available but fragmented documentation. Given the absence of source code, system architecture diagrams, or direct IRCC disclosures, our methodology relied on a distributed archive of legal, journalistic, research, and institutional evidence. These sources provided varying degrees of insight into how Chinook may function, which we used to inform the structural logic, interface design, and speculative elements of our prototype (Daponte, 2021a; Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a; Tao, 2022).

Much of what is known about Chinook comes from litigation-related materials. The Daponte Affidavit (Ocran v. Canada) and its accompanying exhibits outline the basic modules of Chinook, including File Management, Pre-Assessment, Decision-Maker, Post-Decision, and Indicator Management (Daponte, 2021a). The cross-examination of Andie Daponte added critical clarification regarding discretionary use, refusal note templates, and the use (and deletion) of working notes (Daponte, 2021b). These materials provided our clearest view of the system’s logic, workflows, and institutional intent.

This legal foundation was complemented by multiple Federal Court rulings, which fall into two lines. In Safarian v. Canada and Khosravi v. Canada, decided by Justice Grammond within a week of each other, the Court set the refusals aside. It held that boilerplate reasoning is not objectionable in itself, but that a reviewing court must be satisfied the officer turned their mind to the facts of the case, and observed in Khosravi that if an assisted decision-making tool gives an officer a truncated view of an application, the resulting decision may well be unreasonable (Khosravi, 2023; Safarian, 2023). A second line of cases has been less receptive. In Jamali, Shirkavand, and Zargar, the Court held that the mere use of Chinook, without evidence that it led to an unfair decision, does not establish a breach of procedural fairness, while declining to rule out that such issues could arise on a fuller evidentiary record (Jamali, 2023; Shirkavand, 2023; Zargar, 2023).

The reasoning in that second line begins earlier, with Haghshenas v. Canada and Raja v. Canada, both challenges to C11 work permit refusals covering entrepreneurs and the self-employed. In Haghshenas the Court accepted that the decision had input assembled by artificial intelligence, but held that judicial review is concerned with the reasonableness of the decision an officer made, whether or not such tools were used. In Raja the Court found no evidence connecting the use of Chinook to a breach of fairness in the officer's assessment, while indicating that such an argument remained open on a proper record (Haghshenas, 2023; Raja, 2023).

Ocran is significant for a different reason. In dismissing the application on other grounds, the Court left open the question of whether a certified tribunal record is deficient when Chinook spreadsheets are neither retained nor included in it, an issue that goes directly to what the system records and what it discards (Ocran, 2022). Taken together, these decisions are valuable less for their outcomes than for the descriptions of Chinook they place on the record, including how it interfaces with the Global Case Management System used by IRCC and how it presents applications to officers in aggregate. These judicial references helped us infer the probable function of interface components, such as toggle-driven refusal sections and editable note fields, which we then reconstructed in our speculative prototype.

In parallel, Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP)-released documents such as the Chinook 1.5 user manual and internal training decks allowed us to visualize partial screenshots, field labels, and interface behaviors (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a, 2021b). While many portions of these documents were redacted, enough structural detail remained to suggest how officers might navigate through different modules, and how indicators or risk flags were managed across cases. These training materials frequently referenced “like-case” logic (batching/grouping applications with similar attributes for streamlined processing), dropdown categorization, and pre-assessment shortcuts, all of which influenced how our interface was built in Figma.

Beyond court and training documents, we consulted official records from the House of Commons Standing Committee on Citizenship and Immigration (CIMM), especially the February 2022 sessions that addressed the development and implementation of Chinook (Zahid, 2022). Government officials repeatedly emphasized that Chinook is “not artificial intelligence,” yet described operational behaviors, such as risk-based sorting and refusal generation, that functionally resemble automated decision support. This rhetorical distancing from AI terminology informed our decision not to visually depict Chinook as algorithmic, but rather as an acceleration layer over human judgment constrained by interface defaults. However, we also recognize that the insistence of federal officials that Chinook is not AI may work to shield Chinook from the accountability mechanisms in place for systems that are labeled AI. Côté-Boucher and Paquet (2026) show that this framing proved effective: as the dispute moved from immigration lawyers into media and parliamentary debate, the question of whether Chinook constituted artificial intelligence displaced the original concerns about procedural fairness, leaving the department's account of the tool largely intact.

In addition to official records and court disclosures, legal commentary and public-facing blogs provided important interpretive context, especially where formal documentation was silent or ambiguous. Much of this perspective was drawn from the writings of immigration lawyer Will Tao, whose detailed commentaries helped interpret the policy implications of Chinook’s deployment (Tao, 2022). His reflections on transparency, fairness, and due process framed the ethical stakes of our design fiction, grounding it in lived practitioner concerns. Tao's blog and Meurrens Law further contributed insight by tracking public statements from IRCC, refusal rate trends, and evolving government rhetoric about Chinook's role in application triaging (Tao, 2022; Meurrens Law, 2024). Other critical reflections, such as those from Meurrens Law, outlined the rise of advanced analytics and automation within Canadian immigration, reinforcing our decision to position Chinook not as an anomaly, but as part of a broader shift toward computational governance (Meurrens Law, 2024). These legal and media sources did not supply interface details, but were instrumental in tracing patterns of concern that informed the speculative direction and tone of our prototype.

div.head: Drawing Boards for the Design Fiction of Chinook
div.p: Before any digital mockups or video explainers were produced, the foundation of the Chinook design fiction was built on drawing boards, literal and conceptual. These spaces, whether whiteboards in shared rooms or digital sketchpads during calls, became our initial laboratory for making sense of the evidence. They also allowed us to think aloud, sketch freely, and test the spatial logic of the interface as described in the aforementioned fragmented documents.

The process was grounded in collaboration. Team members reviewed legal affidavits, court decisions, redacted training manuals, and policy briefings together, line by line, while actively translating excerpts into sketched components. For instance, when the Daponte affidavit described the “Decision Maker Module” we paused to ask: what might that actually look like? Where would it appear on screen? What kind of input or toggle would the officer use? Each question became a sketch, and each sketch was tested against other parts of the evidence to check for consistency or contradiction (Daponte, 2021a; Daponte, 2021b).

This phase was deeply iterative. We routinely circled back from the drawing board to the documents and back again, using the visual space as a kind of evidence map. Sometimes we revised interface sketches based on a new line discovered in a court decision (Khosravi, 2023; Safarian, 2023). At other times, a note scribbled on the board raised questions that sent us back to the documents for clarification. As Galey, Ruecker, and Ruecker (2010) put it, evidence informed the sketches, and sketches in turn reshaped how we interpreted the evidence.

The drawing board process was not just preparatory. It was a crucial interpretive step that gave form to otherwise abstract or bureaucratic language. It let us work through ambiguity with others, flag contradictions, and surface new lines of inquiry before anything was formalized. More importantly, it made visible our commitments: to transparency, to careful reading, and to treating speculation as disciplined public inquiry, not as fantasy (Blythe, 2014; Dunne and Raby, 2013). At the same time, we fully recognize that our reconstruction may not completely capture Chinook as it operates in practice. By explicitly marking uncertainties and sharing provisional interpretations, we aim to invite feedback and correction, positioning the prototype as an open contribution to ongoing dialogue rather than a final or authoritative account.

figure.figDesc: Hand-drawn sketches tracing an officer's path from login through data selection to the Decision Maker, with the sorting, refusal-reason, and column set-up panels mapped around it, showing how documentary language was first translated into spatial layout.

div.p: This early stage also clarified the limits of the available information. By sketching directly from the language of the documents, we confronted the gaps, omissions, and redactions embedded in official records (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a; Daponte, 2021a). Some modules could be diagrammed with relative confidence, while others remained vague, requiring conditional interpretations. Rather than resolving these uncertainties prematurely, we used the boards to hold multiple possibilities in parallel, treating ambiguity as a methodological resource rather than a flaw (Galey, Ruecker, and Ruecker, 2010; Gaver, 2012).

The redactions became a design problem in their own right, and working through them taught us more than reading around them had. A blacked-out passage in a training manual is not just missing information. On a drawing board it takes up space, and something has to fill it. We could leave the area blank, which would misrepresent a system whose officers clearly see something at that point in the workflow, or we could sketch a plausible component, which would credit the department with a design it has never confirmed. Neither choice is neutral, and a sketch cannot postpone the decision the way a paragraph can, since an interface has no blank spots when someone is using it. Running into this again and again made something clear that reading had not. The redactions are not gaps in an otherwise complete account. They shape the account we have, which means we were never reconstructing Chinook. We were reconstructing Chinook as the state has allowed it to be seen.

In this sense, the drawing boards operated not only as a site of visualization but also as a space for methodological reflection. They helped distinguish what was explicitly stated from what was inferred, and what remained speculative. This allowed us to trace the threshold between evidence and interpretation and to begin building a design fiction that remained accountable to its source material (Blythe, 2017; Coulton et al., 2017; Galloway and Caudwell, 2018).

div.head: Figma Digital Prototype and the Design Fiction of Chinook
div.p: Following the analog sketching phase, the project advanced to digital prototyping using Figma, with a concentrated focus on reconstructing Module 3: Decision Maker. This module received the most consistent and detailed references across internal documentation, court affidavits, and public commentary. It is understood to be the core environment where immigration officers review cases, apply risk indicators, and generate final decisions using standardized refusal templates (Daponte, 2021a; Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a).

Figma was selected for its flexibility in modular interface construction and its ability to support collaborative design and revision. Module 3 was developed using the structure and terminology described in key source materials. Particular attention was given to the arrangement of decision-making fields, drop-downs for boilerplate refusals, embedded notes, and batch processing tools. These elements were anchored in direct references wherever available and were annotated accordingly within the prototype.

Visual fidelity was prioritized for interface elements that had clear correlates in the evidence. Terms like “Refusal Notes,” “Group Numbers,” and “Working Notes” were used verbatim from policy and training documents. Interface groupings, such as applicant summaries, risk indicators, and decision input areas, were laid out based on inferred officer workflows, especially in contexts involving high-volume triage or streamlined refusals.

Where source material lacked specificity, design choices were guided by institutional logic and interface conventions typical of government case management systems (Galloway and Caudwell, 2018). These speculative components were clearly distinguished using visual labels and were cross-referenced with corresponding justification in the project documentation. This method preserved interpretive transparency and emphasized the boundaries of what could be responsibly reconstructed.

Two components were harder to build than we expected, and in both cases the problem turned out to be in the system rather than in our drawing of it. The first was working notes. We know officers write notes while assessing a file, and we know these notes are routinely deleted, leaving little audit trail (Daponte, 2021b; Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a). But an interface has to put the field somewhere, and wherever we put it, it looks like a record. A bordered text box inside a case view reads as documentation. It implies the text will be kept and can be found later. We could not find a way to draw a field whose main institutional feature is that what you write in it disappears. We included it and annotated its status, but the failure is worth stating, because it points to something odd about the tool itself: Chinook gives officers a place to write down reasons that the record does not keep. This is not only our reading. In Mehrara, the Federal Court observed that IRCC's systemic deletion of materials generated by processing technology may not reflect best practice, though it declined to find the omission relevant on the facts before it (Mehrara, 2024; Otchengco, 2025). What we could not draw is a feature the Court has also noticed, without either of us being able to say what the deleted notes contained.

The second was batch processing. The documents describe grouping applications by shared attributes, including citizenship and school, and handling them together (Tao, 2022; Daponte, 2021a). Drawing this meant designing a control, and a control takes the same effort no matter what it does. Ticking a box for forty files is the same gesture as ticking it for one. We could not draw the element in a way that made that difference visible, which is the point: the interface does not make it visible either. The gap between how much the outcome matters to an applicant and how little effort the action takes is not something our reconstruction introduced. It is how the tool works.

A third problem ran through the whole phase. IRCC says Chinook is not artificial intelligence, while the same documents describe risk-based sorting and refusal generation (Zahid, 2022; Côté-Boucher and Paquet, 2026). There is no standard way to draw that combination, and an image cannot hold a contradiction the way a sentence can. Our solution, showing an acceleration layer over human judgment constrained by interface defaults, is a position we had to take, not one the department has stated. Having to draw something forced us to settle a question the documents leave open.

The prototype evolved through multiple revision cycles. As additional evidence was incorporated or inconsistencies were identified, the interface design was adjusted for coherence and plausibility. Figma’s component system enabled efficient updates across screens, ensuring uniformity while allowing for iterative refinement. Each revision was tracked and aligned with updates to the video explainer and documentation, maintaining internal consistency across project outputs.

By the end of this phase, the digital prototype offered a structured and interpretable reconstruction of Module 3. It does not simulate decision-making outcomes but instead visualizes how such decisions may be operationalized within a semi-automated workflow.

div.head: Making the Design Fiction of Chinook Publicly Legible: Video Production
div.p: To more widely share the speculative interface reconstruction, a 20-minute explainer video See Chinook explainer video (2025), Chinook Design Fiction Video – V02 [Video]. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1OaAPKZtOnqN02zmnaDzIdYV5-2xgZcY0/view. was developed to communicate Chinook’s seeming operational logic to a broader public audience, especially those affected by Chinook. This phase translated the design fiction and supporting research into a narrative format that emphasized accessibility, clarity, and evidence-based reconstruction.

The storyboard was constructed based on the modular logic of the system, with particular focus on Module 3 (Decision Maker). Sequences were developed to depict key components and workflows as described in affidavits, internal manuals, and court testimony (Daponte, 2021a; Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 2021a). Each scene was anchored in available evidence, visualized through the Figma prototype, and narrated using a plain-language voiceover with commentary drawn from the project’s documentation and legal commentary.

Fictional placeholders were introduced for illustrative purposes. An officer named “John” and an applicant named “Alex” served as narrative anchors to visualize both the interface and its implications for temporary resident visa applicants. These characters framed the system’s operation from administrative and applicant-facing perspectives.

Scenes were structured to walk viewers through login procedures, dashboard configuration, batch processing, attribute-based filtering (e.g., by citizenship or school), use of risk indicators, and the generation of refusal notes using standardized templates. Animations were derived directly from the digital prototype to ensure alignment between the storyboard and the interface. Interface behaviors, such as toggling indicators, adjusting columns, and exporting decisions, were illustrated through simulated interactions based on institutional logic and described functionality.

Throughout production, annotations and disclaimers were integrated to distinguish confirmed features from speculative ones. These distinctions were reinforced through visual markers, voiceover language, and supporting documents. The video also included cues for cross-referencing scenes with relevant documentation, ensuring coherence across all project outputs.

div.head: Assessing the Strengths and Limitations of Design Fiction and the case of Chinook
div.p: The use of design fiction in this project revealed several methodological strengths, particularly in addressing the challenges of studying an opaque digital system like Chinook. One of the most significant strengths was its ability to render the operations of a black-boxed system interpretable and accessible to researchers across disciplines and the broader public. By visualizing possible interface elements and workflows, the project translated abstract legal and bureaucratic concepts into concrete, navigable designs. This made it possible to engage audiences, including those outside of legal or policy circles, in meaningful critique and discussion.

Another key strength was the method’s capacity to synthesize fragmented and heterogeneous forms of evidence. Legal affidavits, redacted training manuals, Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) disclosures, and media commentary were all integrated into a shared design logic. The visual and iterative nature of the prototyping process helped the team triangulate across sources, testing how interface components described in one context aligned or contradicted with details from others.

At the same time, the approach made explicit its own assumptions and interpretive leaps. Speculative elements were consistently marked, annotated, and documented, reinforcing a norm of transparency rather than authority. In this way, the design fiction methodology encouraged reflexivity. It foregrounded the interpretive labor of the researchers and invited readers and viewers to question what is known, what is inferred, and what remains concealed. The speculative prototype did not pretend to represent Chinook in full fidelity. Rather, it was a vehicle to pose difficult questions about how power is encoded in software systems.

Design fiction also helps to visualize and interrogate opaque systems in the absence of source code, insider access, or detailed technical documentation. It allowed for the synthesis of disparate forms of evidence, legal, technical, policy, and narrative, into a coherent interface logic. This synthesis was not neutral. Every design choice was embedded with assumptions, which is why iterative documentation, internal peer review, and public annotation were integral throughout the process.

Design fiction also helped surface ethical questions not always visible in textual analysis alone. By placing speculative users into reconstructed workflows, the design raises questions about discretion, accountability, and automation that were otherwise dispersed across court documents and policy briefings. The speculative lens, in this way, made visible the affective and procedural stakes of decision-making systems, reinforcing critiques raised by legal advocates and civil society organizations (Tao, 2022).

The most useful strength of all, however, was the friction the method produced. Building an interface does not let one skip past things the way writing does. A sentence can note that working notes are deleted and move on; a screen has to show where they get written. A paragraph can say applications are processed in groups; a control has to specify what the officer clicks. Each of these requirements brought us to a point where the record was not enough, not because it was redacted, but because what it describes does not add up. The notes field that documents nothing, the control that refuses forty applicants as easily as one, and the system that sorts by risk while officials deny it is artificial intelligence are not readings we brought to the prototype. They are what the prototype would not let us leave unsaid. The reconstruction worked less as an illustration of concerns raised elsewhere and more as a way of finding them, and the oddities it turned up are the everyday operating conditions of a bureaucracy handling a very large volume of applications.

Still, the method carries limitations. Design fiction does not offer empirical verification. Its strength lies in plausibility and interpretive framing, not in technical accuracy. The final prototype does not claim to depict Chinook as it exists when using an IRCC workstation, but rather as it may function based on what is observable from the outside. This distinction was maintained throughout the project by marking speculative components, avoiding deterministic conclusions, and situating all claims within a bounded evidentiary frame (Dunne and Raby, 2013; Barendregt and Vaage, 2021).

Design fiction also raises the risk of over-interpretation. Despite annotations and disclaimers, there is always a possibility that viewers may interpret the design as a literal interface rather than a research artifact that involves speculation. The narrative and visual clarity of the prototype, while useful for accessibility, can inadvertently imply authority. Moreover, this methodology may not generalize easily across other black-boxed systems. Chinook was a viable subject for design fiction because of the volume of related litigation, public records, and insider testimony. In systems where such documentation is unavailable or heavily censored, the speculative method would struggle to meet ethical or evidentiary thresholds.

A further limitation concerns the position from which this critique is made. Our reconstruction addresses a system whose developers have had no part in it, and the account IRCC has given of Chinook's origins deserves to be engaged rather than treated as mere justification. The Daponte affidavit describes Chinook as an in-house response to operational conditions: sharply rising application volumes, and a case management system that performed poorly over the low-bandwidth connections common at visa offices abroad and obliged officers to move between multiple windows to assemble a single file. Chinook was not procured from an external vendor, nor designed as an instrument of automated adjudication. It was built by officers, in Excel, to make an unwieldy system workable against performance targets they did not set (Daponte, 2021a). Read this way, Chinook is less an imposition of algorithmic governance from above than an accumulation of local workarounds that hardened into a new layer of infrastructure, which is a different problem and arguably a more common one.

Taking that account seriously does not blunt our critique so much as relocate it. Whether or not batch processing and templated refusals were intended to constrain discretion, they shape how discretion is exercised, and an efficiency measure that becomes the routine environment of decision-making acquires governing force regardless of the intentions behind it. The question our prototype poses to IRCC is therefore not whether its officers acted in bad faith, but why a tool built to relieve administrative pressure has been shielded from the scrutiny that its effects on applicants would ordinarily invite?.

Two implications follow for design fiction as a form of critique. The first is an asymmetry of response. We reconstructed a system whose developers cannot correct our errors without disclosing the details the department has chosen to withhold, so the same institutional opacity that makes speculation necessary also prevents the people best placed to refute it from doing so. Marking speculative elements and inviting correction are procedural safeguards, but they do not dissolve this asymmetry. The second implication concerns what happens to a speculative artifact once it circulates. A reconstruction that is visually coherent and easy to follow may come to stand in for the system in public debate, displacing the messier object it represents. The Chinook controversy has already shown how readily attention can migrate from the substantive question of procedural fairness to a narrower dispute over whether the tool meets the definition of artificial intelligence, a framing that has served the department well (Côté-Boucher and Paquet, 2026). A design fiction can contribute to that drift as easily as it can resist it, which is why we have tied every element of the prototype to a cited source and treated the reconstruction as an argument to be contested rather than a depiction to be believed.

Maintaining coherence between the written documentation and the animated explainer was central to the methodology. Each segment of the video is linked to a corresponding section of the documentation, enabling viewers to cross-check the visual narrative against cited evidence. The animation serves as an accessible entry point, while the documentation provides detailed context and references.
See Sharifi, Padilla, and Rockwell (2025), Chinook Design Fiction Documentation Appendix, which records the evidentiary source for each interface element depicted. https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Hr22xe9_XZEXhcPnXnVEdsGsKIN1Hscx.
Together they operated as complementary outputs: the video communicates the system’s speculative logic to a wider public, and the documentation reinforces transparency by showing exactly how each design choice was grounded or marked as uncertain.

Finally, while ambiguity was treated as a resource during the sketching and prototyping phases, it also presented challenges. Ambiguity enabled a more open-ended exploration of possibilities, but it complicated efforts to communicate clear findings to policymakers or the public. Without sufficient framing, speculative work risks being dismissed as conjecture rather than grounded inquiry. In an era often described as “post-truth,” where misinformation and skepticism toward expertise are widespread, this risk becomes even more pronounced. For this reason, every stage of the project emphasized interpretive discipline, cautious language, and consistent citation, even when working within the speculative space.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This article has explored the use of design fiction as a methodological tool for the critical modeling and examination of Chinook, an internal decision-support system used by the IRCC. By grounding our speculative reconstruction in court affidavits, redacted training manuals, and legal commentary, we were able to prototype Chinook’s Decision Maker module (module 3) and visualize how its interface may influence visa decision-making processes.

Each phase of the project (such as drawing board sketching, Figma prototyping, and video production) worked to show the interpretation required when dealing with partial, contradictory, or deliberately redacted information. The interpretive work was also confrontational. At each stage, having to build something specific exposed features of the system that its own documentation records without seeming to notice. This is where the urgency of the case is clearest: not in the fact that Chinook is hidden, but in what shows up as soon as anyone tries to draw it. The resulting design fiction is not a claim to technical accuracy but a structured provocation, meant to invite scrutiny and encourage deeper public engagement with the procedural realities of the digital shift in immigration governance. This approach acknowledges the evidentiary limits of working from the outside while also affirming the importance of critical inquiry, especially when democratic oversight is also limited.

By treating design fiction as both critique and inquiry, the article contributes to broader debates in digital humanities and beyond about methods, algorithmic governance, digital bureaucracy, and public accountability. Methodologically, this article contributes to how design fiction is usually practiced. Rather than speculating from imagination, we speculated from the available documents such as affidavits, ATIP releases, and court rulings. These documents served as the evidentiary spine of the reconstruction and marked the point at which that record gave out. Second, rather than directing speculation at an emerging technology, we directed it at a bureaucratic system already in operation, where the object of inquiry is not a possible future but a concealed present. Design fiction, practiced this way, becomes a method of evidentiary reconstruction suited to institutions that are documented but not disclosed. In doing so, this article complements and extends work in digital humanities, human-computer interaction, socio-legal studies, and policy studies concerned with the ethics of automation and the infrastructures of state power.

Future interdisciplinary research may build on this method to explore other black-boxed systems across policy domains, including education, healthcare, or border security. As decision-making processes become increasingly data-driven and interface-mediated, speculative reconstruction can help scholars from various disciplines, advocates, and affected communities interrogate the tools that shape access to rights and resources and powerfully determine life chances. Even emerging fields such as quantum computing, with their potential to reshape data processing at scale, may benefit from speculative engagement to surface assumptions before these systems solidify into institutional norms.
